rationale: B wins because it keeps a tighter leash on the unknowns. Its strongest line, "Whoop puts a cleared ECG and an uncleared blood-pressure estimate on the same wrist," is a real beat story and its proof demands are sharp enough to stop a founder from pitching vapor. A is useful, but "catch-up-and-leapfrog story" and "Cuffless blood pressure is the next wearable battleground" run past the supplied facts; the update does not prove leapfrogging or a category battleground.
gaps_in_A: "catch-up-and-leapfrog story" is the main offense. The facts say competitors already have cleared ECG and Whoop has a wellness BP estimate; they do not prove Whoop is leapfrogging anyone.
"Cuffless blood pressure is the next wearable battleground" is too big for the evidence supplied. It may be true, but this update alone does not establish the market has moved there.
"the average wearer can't tell the difference" asserts user confusion without evidence. Make it a reporter question, not a fact.
The fourth angle partially duplicates the first and second: BP-as-next-edge plus wellness asterisk appears in both, so the set is a little padded.
gaps_in_B: "What Whoop's cardiologists actually signed off on" overstates the fact block. It says the advisory board reviewed the features; review is not sign-off.
"Whoop is offering a cardiologist advisory board as reassurance" is an inference, not a supplied fact. It needs a company statement or launch material before it can carry an angle.
"false positives, worried-well referrals" is beat-smart context, but it is not in the update. Keep it framed as what the reporter will test, not what this launch has already caused.
"what a privately held company last valued at $3.6B needs from parity to hold a subscription base" assumes competitive retention pressure. Plausible, but still needs subscriber or market evidence.
